opening.headline: I said, ‘Please write well,’ but the reason why the results are different every time is explained from the perspective of finding and filling in the missing elements in the instructions.
body: Even if you make the same request, sometimes you get a two-line summary, sometimes you get a table, and sometimes you get a long text. This is not because the model is incompetent, but because there is a lot of missing information in the request, so each person guesses the length, format, and audience differently.

In this lesson, we will look at the elements of good instruction one by one. These elements include clear and specific instructions, roles and background, examples, output format, task steps, separators and tags. Next, I organize the common directions pointed by Claude, Gemini, and OpenAI's prompt guides into a table, and at the end, I find the missing elements in the bad instruction, 'Prepare the meeting minutes,' and fill them in and rewrite them one by one.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain role, background, instructions, examples, and output format elements
Can find missing elements in ambiguous requests
Can explain the role and priority of system prompts, user messages, and assistant messages
This explains the point that delimiters and tags reduce prompt injection, but do not prevent it completely.

screens.title: I said, ‘Write it well,’ but it’s different every time.
screens.lead: This is a scene where the same request resulted in three completely different results. Read below and think about what was missing.

visual.alt: A scene where three different response cards to the same request ‘Write a good report’ are placed side by side.

paragraphs: An employee who had to submit a report to his boss asked AI to ‘write the report well.’ The first response was a two-line summary, the second a table, and the third a long, slick essay. It was the same request, but the results were all different.

The model is not arbitrary or incompetent. This is because the request did not specify anything about what the 'report' was, who would read it, how long it should be, and whether it was a table or text. The model guessed the missing information differently each time, and the guesses resulted in different results.

The question for this class is this. What elements were missing, and how would they be filled in to stabilize the results? The starting point of this class is to develop an eye for finding missing elements.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The word ‘well’ is concrete only in the mind of the person asking it. What would it take to translate that standard into words the model can understand?

screens.outro: Now let's start by looking back at the instructions you've written.

screens.title: Looking back at the instructions I wrote
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had to repeat a request several times when the results were not what you expected?
items.answer: The more times you ask again, the more likely it is that there was more information missing from the initial instructions. If you're fixing the same part every time, that's an element missing from the instructions. In this class, you will learn how to name and call the elements.

items.prompt: If I showed my request out of context to a colleague, would they understand?
items.answer: The Claude Prompt Guide introduces this question as a golden rule. If you show a prompt to a colleague with little background on the task and ask him to follow along, and he is confused, then the model will be confused as well. This standard is the inspection tool for this entire class.

items.prompt: Have you ever said 'I'll figure it out' without telling you what format you wanted?
items.answer: ‘Do it yourself’ is the most expensive word. The length, format, and tone are determined by the model, so the results will vary every time. Just writing down the desired shape in one line will greatly reduce shaking.

screens.outro: Let's start with the first element, taking the criterion of colleagues without context.

screens.title: Structure of API calls: System prompts and message roles
screens.lead: Read on for a hypothetical example of what an invisible request looks like in a chat app. See what each line does in the description on the right. This screen is for reading purposes only and is not intended for direct execution.

notes.note: The chat app and API are separate usage paths. APIs are a way for programs to call models directly, and OpenAI help explains that API usage is billed separately from your ChatGPT subscription. Fees vary by model and feature and are based on input and output token usage. Each provider has a different payment system, so you should check the billing method for the service you are using. This example is an assumption to illustrate the structure; actual field names may vary by provider.

system is a system prompt that specifies roles and rules to be followed throughout the conversation. Anthropic Messages API receives this as a top-level parameter outside of messages, Gemini receives it as system_instruction, and OpenAI receives it as an instructions parameter or a message for the developer role. Even though the name is different, it is the same place. The OpenAI API documentation explains that instructions from the developer or system role take precedence over instructions from the user role. So, the rules to be followed are placed here, and changes made by the user are placed in the user message.

A user message is a request sent by a person. The model receives input in the form of a dialogue between the user and the assistant. The last user message is the question that needs to be answered now, and what lies ahead is the context of the conversation.

An assistant message is a response previously made by the model. The model does not remember conversations between requests, so it sends user and assistant messages from previous conversations along with messages in each request. This is why the longer the conversation, the more inputs you send and the more input tokens you use.

This structure is not visible in chat apps. You can understand that the app's user guidelines, project guidelines, and organizational guidelines are text corresponding to the system position in structure, and the content of the conversation corresponds to user and assistant messages. This is not a literal description of the internal implementation, but rather a response to understand its role. Knowing this structure allows you to read where subsequent prompt elements fit.

screens.outro: Now that you know the structure of a request, let's take a look at how to write clear and specific instructions within it.

screens.title: Clear and specific instructions, roles and background
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the same request differs when it is ambiguous and when it is concrete.

visual.alt: A side-by-side comparison of vague instructions on the left and specific, element-filled instructions on the right.

states.label: Ambiguity
states.body:
The request is one line: ‘Write a good report.’ This one line doesn't say what the report is, who reads it, or how long it should be.

The Claude Prompt Guide compares Claude to a new employee who is great but doesn't know our norms and how we work. This means that the more accurately you explain what you want, the better the results. If you show these instructions to a colleague without context, he or she will immediately ask you back. What kind of report it is, how many pages it is, and who reads it. Instructions that are confusing to your colleague are also confusing to the model.

The Gemini guide also explains instructions by dividing them into types such as questions, tasks, targets, and continuation input, and instructs you to write down constraints such as length along with the instructions. Ambiguous instructions are missing this element.

states.label: materialization
states.body:
Replace the same request like this: ‘You are the secretary who organizes the sales team’s weekly reports. This report is read by the absent team leader within 3 minutes. 'Please write down three accomplishments from last week and two plans for this week on one page.'

It contains three devices: The first is role. Claude's guide explains that simply giving a single sentence to the system prompt brings together the model's behavior and tone.

Second is the background and reason. The guide says that if you write down the reason for your instruction, the model will generalize your intent. For example, rather than ‘Do not use ellipsis,’ it is better to say, ‘The voice engine for reading aloud cannot read ellipsis, so do not use it.’ In this case, the reason it can be read in 3 minutes is the basis for writing it briefly.

Third is a specific request. The figures of three achievements, two plans, and one page determine the length.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the basic elements, let's move on to examples and output formats that determine what the results will look like.

screens.title: Provide examples and specify output format
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the rules for when there are no examples, when there are examples, and when to use examples.

tabs.label: No example (zero-shot)
tabs.body:
The Gemini Guide calls a prompt without an example a zero-shot. Just write, ‘Organize the meeting contents in a table,’ and the model determines the column names, number of columns, and sentence length. Sometimes there are three ten, sometimes there are five.

If the instructions are simple and the model is already good at a task, a zero-shot is sufficient. However, if the shape of the result must be the same every time, it is more accurate to show it than to explain it in words.

tabs.label: Example (few-shot)
tabs.body:
Adding an example or two is a few-shot. The Gemini Guide explains that examples are used to achieve format, expression, and scope. If the example is clear enough, you can shorten some of the instructions.

Claude's guide states that there are three conditions for a good example. It has a structure that resembles actual use cases, diversity that encompasses boundary cases, and a `<example>` tag to differentiate it from instructions.

```
<example>
Input: Manager Kim will send out the quotation by next Monday.
Output: | Send quotation | Assistant Manager Kim | Next Monday |
</example>
```

tabs.label: Rules of Example
tabs.body:
Examples must have the same format as each other. The Gemini guide even tells you to match XML tags, spaces, line breaks, and delimiters. If the format is different for each example, the model will not know which one to follow, and the output will be inconsistent.

Additionally, having too many examples can lead to overfitting, where the response becomes too tailored to the examples. The appropriate number is found by experiment.

You specify the output format yourself, such as table, bullet, or single sentence. You can also write down the beginning of the response in advance and write it down afterwards. The Gemini guide calls this partial input completion, and explains that if you give an example and a response prefix together, the model will follow the format exactly. For tasks where formality is important, it is safer to show one item in person rather than explain it verbally.

screens.outro: Now that you've seen the format and examples, let's look at how to break down tasks into steps and differentiate them.

screens.title: Dividing work into steps, separators and tags
screens.lead: Select the arrows to move through each step and watch the prompt building blocks stack up one by one.

visual.alt: Illustration of a prompt structure with the Role, Background, Instructions, Examples, Input, and Format blocks stacked from top to bottom.
labels: Instructions are outside the tag, input is inside the tag.

steps.title: Role and background at the forefront
steps.body: The prompt begins by telling the model who he or she is working for. Even a single sentence in the system prompt captures the model's behavior and tone. The background is a sentence or two that tells you who will write the results and how.

steps.title: Tasks that have an order are divided by number.
steps.body: Claude guides you to write your steps in order, either as a numbered list or as bullets, if order or omission is important to you. For example, '1. If you write things like ‘Extract decisions 2. Assign a person in charge 3. Check deadlines’, the model will not skip any steps.

steps.title: Surround examples with tags
steps.body: Claude's guide recommends wrapping examples with the tag `<example>` and multiple examples with the tag `<examples>`. The model then distinguishes examples from instructions. It is important to be consistent in using the same tags and delimiters in each example.

steps.title: Put the input inside a tag
steps.body: The guide explains that in prompts that mix instructions, context, examples, and variable input, wrapping each piece of content in its own tag reduces interpretation errors. Write names like `<instructions>`, `<context>`, and `<input>` and keep them consistent throughout the prompts. Long inputs, such as the original meeting text, are placed inside tags such as `<meeting_notes>`, and instructions are placed outside the tags.

steps.title: Tags are not a complete defense
steps.body:
If sentences that read like instructions are mixed into unbelievable text, such as an external document, web page, or email, the model can follow the sentences. This phenomenon is called prompt injection. Wrapping input with tags reduces risk by making it easier for the model to distinguish between instructions and data, but it does not completely prevent it. OWASP puts prompt injection on the list of top risks for LLM applications, explaining that the model's output is inherently probabilistic, making it unclear whether full prevention is even possible.

So, when inserting an external document that is difficult to trust, keep all three together. First, write in the instructions that sentences in the document should only be read as information and not executed. Second, limit permissions so that responses do not lead to actual actions such as sending or deleting mail. Third, there is a step where the results are verified by a human.

steps.title: Divide the priority of instructions
steps.body: The OpenAI Prompt Guide explains that if instructions are given in the API as `instructions` parameters or developer messages, they will take precedence over the user message of `input`. The rules to be followed are placed here, and the inputs that the user changes are placed separately.

steps.title: Check with snapshots
steps.body: OpenAI informs you that even for the same model family, results may vary depending on the snapshot. So I recommend checking and evaluating the prompts with a fixed snapshot. Even well-written prompts need to be revisited when the model changes.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed all the elements, we will organize in a table the directions that the three companies' guides commonly point in.

data.notes: The expressions of the three companies are different, but the direction is the same. The idea is to reduce ambiguity, demonstrate expected results, and refine prompts once written through experimentation. Most of the principles learned from one company's guide also apply to other models. However, detailed methods, such as tag names or message role names, vary from company to company, so check the guide for the model you are using. When reading a table, you can use it as a checklist by replacing each row with a question. For example, the five questions are 'Can a person without context follow these instructions?', 'Are there examples?', 'Is the format written down?', 'Are input and instructions separated?', and 'Have they been checked again?' If you can answer 'yes' to all five of these questions, the instructions are generally ready. If you answer 'no' to any one, it means that the corresponding element in that row is missing. By turning principles into questions in this way, they can be checked in the same way even if the model changes.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the common principles, let's dive into the commentary to find the missing elements in bad prompts.

screens.title: Case Study 1: Finding the Missing Elements of Bad Prompts
screens.lead: The instructor checks the one-line instruction, ‘Take the meeting minutes.’ Select the arrows to step through the checklist items one by one.

steps.title: original text
steps.body: The original text to be checked is one line, ‘Please organize the meeting minutes.’ I'm assuming there's a text of the meeting attached underneath it. It's a short and natural request, but if you show it to a co-worker out of context, they'll immediately ask you questions.

steps.title: Check 1: Role and Background
steps.body: There is no information about who the meeting minutes are for or what the purpose of the meeting is. Important details vary depending on whether it is a sales team weekly meeting or a customer meeting. This item is 'None'. A complementary direction is to write down the role, who will read it, and how it will be read.

steps.title: Check 2: Instructions
steps.body: It's unclear whether 'organizing' is a summary, an distillation of decisions, or a to-do list. If the instructions are ambiguous, the model picks the most common interpretation. This item is also 'None'. The complementary direction is to clearly state the desired action in one verb.

steps.title: Check 3: Examples and Format
steps.body: There is no length, tabularity, or item name. I don't know whether the answer will be in lines or a table. There are no examples, so there is no standard for matching the shape. A complementary direction is to specify the format directly and show a pair of inputs and outputs.

steps.title: Check 4: Separator
steps.body: The original text of the meeting and the instructions are all mixed together. If there is a sentence like ‘Please send it to me by next week’ in the meeting content, the model may misunderstand it as an instruction. The direction of supplementation is to put the original text inside the tag and place the instructions outside the tag.

steps.title: Inspection results
steps.body: Each bundle examined lacks the necessary specificity. The following explanation sequentially supplements the roles, background, output format, examples, and delimiters, and also specifies instructions for work to be performed in the final version.

screens.outro: Now that we've found the missing elements, let's go through the process of filling them in and rewriting them one by one.

screens.title: Case Commentary 2: Rewriting by Element
screens.lead: The instructor completes the prompt by adding elements to the original text one by one. Select the arrows to see which sentences grow as elements are added.

steps.title: Add role
steps.body: Add role to the first sentence. 'You are the secretary who organizes the sales team's weekly meetings.' Although it is only one sentence, the model can decide from what position and in what tone it will be written.

steps.title: Add background and reason
steps.body: Add background to the following sentences. 'The results are read within 3 minutes by the team leader who was not present. So, I write briefly and without unnecessary words.' Because the reason is written together, the constraint to write briefly is justified, and the model generalizes judgments other than length in line with this intention.

steps.title: Add output format
steps.body: Specify the format yourself. 'Organize the meeting contents in a table with three columns: decisions, responsible person, and deadline.' Since the column names are set, the table will look the same every time.

steps.title: Add example
steps.body: Put the input and output pair into the `<example>` tag. One example is enough, and the format matches the actual input. If there is an example, even the style of filling in the columns of the table is followed.

steps.title: Add separator
steps.body: Put the original text of the meeting inside the `<meeting_notes>` tag and place the instructions outside the tag. This reduces the likelihood that sentences in the original text will be misunderstood as instructions. However, tags are not a complete defense, so if the original text is difficult to believe, human confirmation is included.

steps.title: Completed Prompt
steps.body:
```
You are the secretary who organizes the sales team's weekly meetings.
The results are read by the absent team leader within 3 minutes. So, I write briefly and without unnecessary words.
Organize your meeting in a three-column table: Decisions, Person in Charge, and Due Date.

<example>
<meeting_notes>Assistant Manager Kim will send the quotation by next Monday</meeting_notes>
<output>| Decisions | Contact person | Deadline |
| Send quotation | Assistant Manager Kim | Next Monday |</output>
</example>

<meeting_notes>
(Paste the original text of the meeting here)
</meeting_notes>
```

Roles, background, instructions, format, examples, and delimiters are all included. The reason it is longer is not because it is wordy, but because it fills in missing elements. The goal is not to write at length, but to write so that colleagues without context can follow along.

screens.outro: Now that I've finished rewriting, I'll summarize the main points of this lesson.

screens.title: Eyes that fill in missing elements
screens.lead: Let's organize the elements covered in this class by connecting them to the first question.

paragraphs: The initial question was what elements were missing and how to fill them in to stabilize the results. Now you have a checklist. Clear and specific instructions, roles and background (including reasons), examples, output format, task steps, separators and tags. All you have to do is write one instruction and then check what's missing from these six items.

The standard for inspection is colleagues without context. If the colleague can read the instructions and follow them without asking again, the model will follow them reliably. Since the three companies' guides point in the same direction, this checklist will work no matter which model you use.

Once you write a prompt, it's not the end. Try changing the number of examples, and check again if the model or snapshot changes. Good instructions are refined through inspection and supplementation rather than being completed all at once. Immediately apply the checklist you learned today to your next instructions.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: The standard for good instructions is not to write at length, but to fill in missing elements.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: When calling a model with an API, output rules to be followed are placed in the developer (or system) message, and requests changed by the user are placed in the user message. If the instructions of two messages conflict, which will take precedence?
options: Directions from the developer or system role take precedence over those from the user role.
Two messages cannot collide and therefore have no priority.
checks.explain: The OpenAI API documentation explains that instructions from the developer or system role take precedence over instructions from the user role. So, here are the rules that must be followed.

wrong.0: This is a structure that places rules in a higher role to prevent user requests from overwriting the rules.
wrong.2: Assistant messages are responses previously made by the model and are not a place to prioritize instructions.
wrong.3: Priorities between roles are established and serve as a basis for when conflicts arise.

checks.q: This is a prompt with three examples, but the delimiters and line breaks for each example are different, so the output format is also uneven. What is the most appropriate prescription?
options: Increase the number of examples to ten or more so that the model learns the average.
Delete all examples and only write longer instructions.
Leave out the output format specification statement and let the model decide it for you.
Match the XML tags, spaces, line breaks, and delimiters in the examples.
checks.explain: Examples are a means of matching format, expression, and scope, so they must have the same format. The output will be stable only if tags, spaces, line breaks, and delimiters match.

wrong.0: Too many examples can result in overfitting the example.
wrong.1: The criterion is not length, but filling in missing elements, and if you erase all examples, you will have no means of showing the format.
wrong.2: If you don't specify the format, you'll end up guessing differently each time, which will lead to more wiggle room.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match the following prompt elements with their effects.
right: Decide on the shape of your response, such as a table, list, or single sentence
Helps the model generalize and determine intent
Reduces misinterpretation of instructions, context, and input mixed together
checks.explain: Background and reasons generalize intent, examples match format and scope, tags break up input to reduce misinterpretation, and formatting sets the shape of the response.
checks.intro: Let’s check what we looked at earlier with one problem. There are no records or grading, so feel free to solve it.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

checks.q: When rewriting the request for meeting minutes, I added the following sentence: ‘The results will be read by the team leader who was not present within 3 minutes.’ What is the biggest role this sentence plays?
options: Divide meeting text and instructions into different chunks
Give reasons for length and format constraints so the model understands your intent.
Forces the format so that the output is always tabular.
The model is given the role of sales team secretary.
checks.explain: By writing down the background and reason, the model generalizes the intent of the constraint. The length restriction is justified by the fact that it must be short and quick to read.

wrong.0: Separation of the original text and instructions is the role of a separator or tag.
wrong.2: Table formatting is handled by a separate output formatting statement.
wrong.3: Role assignment is handled by sentences such as ‘Secretary who organizes the sales team’s weekly meeting.’

checks.intro: Please choose with the intention of organizing what you have learned. Results are not saved.

glossary.def: This is a method of matching the format and expression by adding several examples to the prompt. If there are no examples, it is called a zero-shot.
This is the setting of the stance and tone given to the model through system prompts, etc. Just one sentence brings action.
It is a marker such as an XML tag or title that divides instructions, context, examples, and input.
This involves directly writing down the desired response, such as a table, list, or single sentence.

It is a structure that distinguishes between the system (or developer) position, which sets rules to be followed throughout the conversation in an API request, the user message sent by a person, and the assistant message previously created by the model.
This is a phenomenon in which sentences in an input such as an external document act like instructions and change the model's behavior. You can reduce it to tags, but you can't prevent it completely.

misconceptions.myth: The longer the instructions, the better.
misconceptions.fact: The criterion is not length, but whether missing elements are filled. It is sufficient for colleagues without context to be able to follow along.
If there are too many examples, the response may overfit the examples. Find the appropriate number through experimentation, and match the format of the examples.

misconceptions.myth: A well-written prompt will work the same even if the model changes.
misconceptions.fact: Even for the same model family, results may vary depending on the snapshot. If your model changes, you will need to recheck your prompts.

misconceptions.myth: Wrapping the input with tags completely prevents you from following instructions in the external document.
misconceptions.fact: Tags help the model distinguish between instructions and material, but they are not a complete defense. When inserting documents that are difficult to believe, we include instructions to read them only as data, restrictions on authority, and human verification.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Clear and specific instructions are at a level that even colleagues without context can follow.
Conveying intentions becomes better when you write down the role and background along with the reason.
Examples and output formats are a key means of fixing the appearance of the results, and the formats must match between examples.
Step breaks, separators, and tags reduce misinterpretation and are a common direction in the three companies' guides.
API requests are made with system (or developer), user, and assistant messages, and rules are placed at the highest priority level.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Think of an instruction I often use. What would be the first thing you would ask a colleague without context if you were reading it?
